lines.caption: This is a tour of pull request 61, which makes CI's screenshot uploads and folder checks more reliable, and lets the agent merge.
lines.say: This is a tour of pull request sixty-one, which makes CI's screenshot uploads and folder checks more reliable, and lets the agent merge.

lines.caption: It has three parts: what the PR adds, how it was built and verified, and what comes later.
Part 1. What this PR adds.
Three small fixes, each from its own issue: upload retries, gvfs in the verify job, and a merge rule.
First lane, one upload. The script commits the file, and on success prints the commit's sha, as before.
When the commit fails, the script now sorts the error: a clash, a real error, or a passing GitHub hiccup.
After a hiccup, it first checks whether the file already landed on the shots branch. If so, it uses that commit.
Otherwise it waits and tries again, up to six times, within a five-minute budget for the whole upload step.
Second lane, the verify job. It now installs gvfs with the other test tools.
Each test's own message bus then starts the metadata store, so folder settings reach the disk.
So the search test for issue 21 runs its on-disk and restart checks instead of skipping them.
Third lane, merging. The agent checks a gate: every job green, no open findings, and a passing visual check.
When the gate holds, the agent squash-merges its own pull request, with the usual title.
Otherwise it stops and asks you, for example when a finding needs a decision or CI keeps failing.
Why: on pull request 51, six of about ten runs lost screenshots, although every test passed.
An upload can succeed even when GitHub's answer is lost, so retrying blindly could commit the file twice.
Clashes are retried, real errors like a bad token fail at once, and everything else counts as a hiccup.
The landed check compares the file's blob on the shots branch with the local file's hash.
The gate also needs CI run on the current main, and checks that the jobs really ran rather than skipped.
Upstream merges, and pull requests the agent didn't open, stay yours to merge.
Before, server errors, rate limits and empty answers failed at once. Now they are retried.
Other client errors, such as not found or too large, still fail at once.
The pull request changes two CI scripts and the CLAUDE.md file, and adds this page and its narration.
Note that every merge to main makes a release that deploys to your machines, now also after an agent's merge.
Part 2. How it was built and verified.
It was built from the lost uploads on pull request 51, and keeps the retry loop from pull request 45.
lines.say: It was built from the lost uploads on pull request fifty-one, and keeps the retry loop from pull request forty-five.

lines.caption: A stand-in for the GitHub tool replayed hiccups and lost answers. Each upload landed with exactly one commit.
Real errors failed at once, clashes were still retried, and hiccups stopped once the retry budget ran out.
In the cloud session, installing gvfs made folder metadata writable, and the value survived a new session.
The whole verify suite ran in the cloud session with gvfs, before the last upload fix. All five tests passed.
A real hiccup through GitHub's API wasn't tested, since it can't be caused on demand.
Two fresh reviews found four medium and five low findings between them. All were fixed.
The biggest: an outage could have run the verify job out of time, so retries now share a five-minute budget.
The merge rule now also needs review-report green, and CI run on top of the current main.
After the merge, the next real hiccup tests the retry, and the next pull request in this batch tests the merge rule.
Part 3. What comes later: cutting CI minutes.
This is the first of four pull requests: then review costs, build costs, and fewer jobs, each after the last merges.
Next, CI stops reviewing its own fixes and superseded pushes, and reviews at a lighter level.
Then build and verify skip pull requests without code, and the compiler output is cached.
Last, the small jobs fold into bigger ones, and a push to main may reuse its pull request's build.
In short: fewer false failures in CI, a real on-disk check for folder settings, and merges that don't wait on you.
